# Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 36 (Bu-Vb Pc36)

**Section:** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga (bu-vb)

**Title (Pali):** Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya 36
**Title (English, from literature):** Encouraging a monastic to eat after refusing an invitation

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Dutiyapavāraṇā Sikkhāpada* ("The Second Training Rule on Refusal/Invitation") constitutes the thirty-sixth rule in the *Pācittiya* chapter of the Theravāda *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga* [SuttaCentral]. According to the rule, a monk commits an offense requiring confession if he entices or tricks another monk—who has already completed his meal and refused further offers of food—into eating more, with the deliberate aim of finding fault with or criticizing him [SuttaCentral]. As noted in comparative Vinaya analysis, this monastic regulation directly refers back to the situation governed by the preceding rule (*Pācittiya* 35) [Hüsken 1997].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral demonstrate that this rule was preserved across the Vinaya traditions of early Buddhism, with counterparts found in the Prātimokṣa and Vibhaṅga texts of the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda, Mahīśāsaka, Mahāsāṅghika, Dharmaguptaka, and Kāśyapīya lineages in Chinese, Sanskrit, and Tibetan, along with the Pali *Bhikkhu Pātimokkha* and *Parivāra* [SuttaCentral]. SuttaCentral also identifies parallel rules formulated for nuns in several Vinayas [SuttaCentral].
Text-reuse computations from DharmaNexus highlight extensive shared formulary within the Pali canon, showing its strongest affinity with the directly preceding meal rule *Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Pācittiya* 35 (over 4,000 shared characters, §1.28.1_2–2.1.20 ↔ §2.15.1–3.1.18), along with matches in the *Vinayavinicchayaṭīkā*, *Kammakkhandhaka* (Kd 11), and subsequent *Pācittiya* rules [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language automated alignments by DharmaNexus also detect text-reuse with Tibetan Vinaya literature (such as the *Vinayasūtravṛtti* and *Vinaya-uttaragrantha*) and Sanskrit treatises, including Jayarakṣita’s *Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā* and the *Śrāvakabhūmi* [DharmaNexus].
